notes.meaning: Solomon had ten bronze carts made to serve as movable bases for water basins. Each stand was square, measuring about six feet wide and long, and about four and a half feet high. This sturdy height gave the priests easy access to wash parts of the sacrifices.

The sides of each cart were framed with flat panels set between upright border posts. These panels were decorated with artistic figures of lions, oxen, and cherubim, with carved wreaths draped beneath them. These rich designs matched the royal dignity of the temple and honored God with beautiful craftsmanship.

Each cart rested on four bronze wheels with bronze axles, allowing the heavy carts to roll where needed. Corner supports or brackets rose from the frame to hold the large water basin securely in place. Wreaths decorated the metalwork around the supports.

The top of the cart had a round opening that acted as a collar to support the basin. This opening sat within a raised rim about eighteen inches across, with carvings around its edge. Even though the collar holding the basin was round, the main chest of the cart stayed square.

The wheels were set under the side panels and attached to bronze axles, measuring about twenty-seven inches across. They were designed like chariot wheels, with the hubs, spokes, and rims all cast from molten metal. This durable build ensured they could carry the enormous weight of the water.

Four handles or corner supports projected from each stand, cast as a single piece with the frame. These gave strength to the corners and may have served as handles to guide the carts when priests moved them. Making them out of one piece prevented weak joints from breaking under heavy strain.

A circular band about nine inches high sat at the top of each cart to cradle the basin. Carvings of cherubim, lions, and palm trees covered every open surface, framed by garlands of flowers. These figures echoed the carvings on the temple walls, uniting the portable tools with the sacred house of God.

All ten movable stands were cast using the exact same molds and patterns. Every cart shared identical dimensions, weight, and carved decorations. This uniformity brought order and harmony to the temple courts.

Huram made ten large bronze basins, placing one on each wheeled cart. Each basin held about forty baths—around three hundred gallons of water—and measured six feet across. The priests used this water to wash parts of the animal sacrifices, picturing the cleansing needed to approach God.

Solomon arranged five carts on the south side of the temple and five on the north side. The great bronze Sea was placed at the southeast corner of the court. This practical setup gave the priests ready access to water for the sacrifices on both sides of the temple entrance.

Huram finished the final bronze utensils, including ash pots, shovels, and sprinkling bowls. With these tools complete, he finished all the bronze construction he had agreed to do for King Solomon. Every task, from the giant pillars to the small tools, was carried out with extraordinary skill.

These verses summarize the giant bronze pieces Huram cast, beginning with the two grand pillars for the temple porch. They describe the bowl-shaped capitals on top of the pillars, along with two sets of bronze network. Four hundred metal pomegranates hung in double rows to decorate the lattice work.

The summary continues with the ten movable stands, the ten basins, the massive bronze Sea, and the twelve oxen beneath it. It also lists the pots for carrying ashes, shovels for tending the altar, and basins for catching blood. Huram cast every single one of these items out of bright, polished bronze.

King Solomon had all this bronze casting done in the Jordan Valley between Succoth and Zarethan. The thick clay soil in that region was ideal for making earthen molds that could handle molten metal. Casting the metal far from Jerusalem also kept heavy smoke and heat away from the holy city.

Solomon never weighed these bronze objects because there were so many of them and they were so heavy. David had collected vast stores of bronze from his victories, giving Solomon plenty of metal to use freely. The sheer abundance showed how generously the king gave toward the house of the Lord.

The focus shifts inside the temple to the furnishings made of gold. Solomon made the incense altar covered in gold, as well as the golden table where the Bread of the Presence was placed. The bread served as a regular reminder of God's faithful provision for the twelve tribes.

Ten pure gold lampstands were set in the Holy Place, five along the south wall and five along the north wall. They held golden lamps, flower decorations, and tongs for trimming the wicks. These lamps filled the sacred room with bright light, pointing to God as the source of life and truth.

All the small tools used inside the temple were made of pure gold, including basins, wick trimmers, sprinkling bowls, spoons, and incense firepans. Even the door sockets and hinges for the inner sanctuary and outer rooms were fashioned from gold. The unmatched beauty of this metal reflected the absolute holiness of God's presence.

King Solomon completed the entire construction and furnishing of the temple after seven years of work. He then brought in the remaining gold, silver, and vessels that his father David had dedicated, storing them in the temple treasuries. These dedicated gifts were kept safe for future repairs and the ongoing worship of God.
